subtype: Approach: leaving too little time for the train [Revision]
passage: Note from Ayesha, Tushar's mother. On Sunday we nearly missed the last train home. Traffic near the flyover crawled, and we ran onto the platform as the guard raised the flag. Nobody spoke on the ride. On Monday evening Tushar brought me the trip sheet and pointed at a new line he had added at the bottom: LEAVE ONE HOUR EARLIER. "Then traffic can be slow and we are still fine," he said. I asked what else could run late. He added a second line: AUTOS. We are keeping the sheet on the fridge. - Ayesha

qa.q: What line did Tushar add at the bottom of the trip sheet?
qa.a: He added LEAVE ONE HOUR EARLIER.

qa.q: What does Tushar's new line suggest about how he felt after the near miss?
qa.a: He was rattled and wanted to be sure it would not happen again, so he felt determined.

qa.q: What else could the family add to the plan, and why?
qa.a: They could check the traffic before leaving or choose an earlier train, so one slow road does not decide the evening.

qa.q: How might Ayesha see the line Tushar added?
qa.a: Ayesha probably finds it sensible and is proud, since she keeps the sheet on the fridge.

grounding: After nearly missing the last train, the family plans an earlier start and the child adds a buffer line to the plan.

subtype: Approach: looking at what is available before deciding [Thinking]
passage:
Friday. Suraj's teacher asked for a school model by the next Friday. He had no idea what to make, so instead of choosing, he opened the cupboard.
Saturday. On the balcony floor he laid out flat cardboard, bottle caps, a handful of ice-cream sticks and a coil of old wire. "Caps are wheels," said his brother Kunal. Suraj picked up the sticks and wire. "And these are a bridge." He began building a truck crossing a bridge.
Next Thursday. The model stood on his desk, bottle-cap wheels turning. The idea had come from the pile.

qa.q: What materials did Suraj lay out on the balcony?
qa.a: He laid out flat cardboard, bottle caps, ice-cream sticks and old wire.

qa.q: What was Suraj feeling on Friday when he had no idea what to make?
qa.a: Unsure and stuck, which is why he opened the cupboard instead of choosing.

qa.q: What could Suraj try if the pile suggests nothing, and why?
qa.a: He could sketch a few rough ideas or ask Kunal for one, so there is a starting point to match with the materials.

qa.q: How might Kunal see the pile of materials?
qa.a: Kunal spots wheels in the bottle caps straight away, so he sees possibilities quickly and helps the idea along.

grounding: A boy looks over the materials at home and lets them suggest what he can build for a school model.

subtype: Approach: drawing a sketch before cutting [Action]
passage: In the art room I sit next to Irawati, and this afternoon she had one sheet of thick cardboard, the last in the box. She did not touch the scissors. She drew a windmill on plain paper first, blades, tower, base, with numbers beside each part: 12 cm, 8 cm. Then she cut paper shapes and laid them over the cardboard like a jigsaw. Two blades overlapped, so she moved the tower. Only then did she cut the cardboard, slowly, with no scraps wasted. I would have cut straight away. I cannot say what she felt, but she hummed. - Arnab

qa.q: What did Irawati do before touching the scissors?
qa.a: She drew a windmill on plain paper with numbers beside each part.

qa.q: What might Irawati have been feeling as she worked, and how can Arnab tell?
qa.a: She may have felt calm and focused, since she hummed, though Arnab cannot be sure.

qa.q: What other approach could avoid wasting the cardboard, and why?
qa.a: She could make a full-size mock-up from scrap paper first, so mistakes cost nothing.

qa.q: How does Arnab see Irawati's method compared with Arnab's own?
qa.a: Arnab would have cut straight away, so Arnab finds her method careful and quietly impressive.

grounding: A girl draws a windmill with measurements before cutting, to avoid wasting the only thick sheet of cardboard.

subtype: Approach: trial and error with glue and tape [Action]
passage:
"It tipped again!" Shankar lifted the bottle boat out of the bucket, water dripping.
"Because the tape is on top," said his brother Chetan. "The weight is up high."
"Then I'll tape them side by side." Splash. "Better! But it leans."
"Put a pebble in the middle."
"Here?" The boat wobbled, then settled. Shankar held his breath. Both boys leaned over the bucket. It floated, steady, spinning slowly in the water.
"Design three," said Chetan. "Write it down."

qa.q: Which design floated steadily?
qa.a: Design three floated steadily, with the bottles side by side and a pebble in the middle.

qa.q: What was Shankar feeling as he held his breath over the bucket?
qa.a: Nervous and hopeful, waiting to see whether the boat would finally stay up.

qa.q: What could Shankar do next to test the boat further, and why?
qa.a: He could add small loads one at a time and see how much the boat holds, so he learns its limits.

qa.q: How does Chetan see Shankar's tries?
qa.a: Chetan is helpful and encouraging, offering fixes while letting Shankar do the testing, and he asks him to write down what worked.

grounding: A child tries different ways to join two bottles into a boat, testing each in a bucket until one floats without tipping.

subtype: Approach: copying a video without adapting it [Pitfall]
passage: In the school craft club, Lalit propped a tablet against a pencil box and pressed play on a video about building a crane. The video used a motor, a battery pack and plastic gears. Lalit had none of them. He pushed on anyway, gluing straws where the gears should go, and by the end the arm sagged and flopped. He kicked the table leg. Deepak Sir strolled over, looked at the video, then at the table. "What here could do the job of a gear?" Lalit stared at a bottle cap and a rubber band. Ten minutes later a rubber-band pulley lifted a paper clip, and Lalit grinned.

qa.q: What did the video use that Lalit did not have?
qa.a: It used a motor, a battery pack and plastic gears.

qa.q: What was Lalit feeling when the arm sagged and flopped?
qa.a: Frustrated and angry, since he kicked the table leg.

qa.q: What could Lalit do at the start next time, and why?
qa.a: He could check which materials he has and adapt the plan before copying, using the video for ideas and not as a recipe.

qa.q: How does Deepak Sir see the problem?
qa.a: Deepak Sir sees a boy copying without adapting, so he asks what on the table could do the job.

grounding: A boy follows a video needing parts he lacks, gets stuck, then replaces them with what is at hand and the model works.

subtype: Approach: reusing an object for a new purpose [Thinking]
passage: Behind the tea shop in her village, Noor found a broken umbrella tossed near the ditch, its handle snapped. Her friend Omkar was already laughing. "Rubbish." Noor turned it over. The metal ribs spread like the bones of a fan, and the black cloth hung in tatters. "Look," she said slowly. "If I take off the handle and hang it upside down, the ribs are a frame. Put the cloth over them and it's a lampshade." She carried it home under her arm and that evening fitted it over the bulb holder in the veranda, the ribs throwing round shadows on the wall. Omkar stopped laughing.

qa.q: What did Noor find behind the tea shop?
qa.a: She found a broken umbrella near the ditch.

qa.q: What was Noor feeling as she turned the umbrella over and spoke slowly?
qa.a: Curious and excited, since she was starting to see a new use for it.

qa.q: What else could Noor make from the umbrella parts, and why?
qa.a: She could use the handle as a hook or the cloth for a cover, since each part has a use apart from the umbrella.

qa.q: How might Omkar have seen the umbrella at first?
qa.a: Omkar saw rubbish and laughed, but stopped laughing once the lampshade took shape.

grounding: A girl sees a broken umbrella and realises its ribs and cloth can become a lampshade, a use different from its original purpose.

subtype: Approach: testing a small version first [Action]
passage: In the corner of our classroom, Omkar was building a bridge with ice-cream sticks, but he did not build the whole thing. He glued a short piece between two books and hung small bags of coins from the middle. When the middle bent and the glue cracked, he wrote the number of coins in his notebook. Then he glued two extra sticks under the middle in a triangle and tried again. It held more coins. I asked why he did not just build the big one. "If the big one broke, I'd lose all my sticks." I thought that was clever. I don't know if he was nervous. - Rajni

qa.q: What did Omkar hang from the middle of the short bridge?
qa.a: He hung small bags of coins.

qa.q: What might Omkar have been thinking when he wrote the number of coins?
qa.a: He was probably noting where the bridge fails so he could learn from it, and seemed careful rather than upset.

qa.q: What else could Omkar test on the small bridge, and why?
qa.a: He could try different spacing or glue on the small piece, so the best way is found before the big one is built.

qa.q: How does Rajni see Omkar's method?
qa.a: Rajni thinks it clever, but does not know whether Omkar felt nervous.

grounding: A boy tests a short span first by hanging weights, and learns the middle needs extra support.

subtype: Approach: model collapses and is redesigned [Revision]
passage: My tower of cardboard tubes was as tall as my chair, and on Tuesday it fell over with a slow, sad crumple. Harsha laughed, and I nearly cried. Then I looked at the bottom: three thin tubes, close together, holding up all of it. "The feet are too close together," I thought. I found a shoebox lid, cut out a square frame and glued the tubes to its corners, spreading them wider. Then I built up again, slowly. On Wednesday morning it was still standing, wobbling only when Harsha sneezed. - Kalyani

qa.q: What did Kalyani use to widen the base?
qa.a: Kalyani used a square frame cut from a shoebox lid.

qa.q: What did Kalyani feel when the tower fell?
qa.a: Upset, nearly to the point of crying, and then thoughtful enough to look at the bottom.

qa.q: What other fix might work for a tower that falls, and why?
qa.a: Kalyani could make the tower shorter or add weight low down, since a low centre is steadier.

qa.q: How might Harsha have seen the collapse?
qa.a: Harsha laughed, perhaps in surprise, and may not have meant to hurt, though Kalyani nearly cried.

grounding: A tower of cardboard tubes falls, and the maker decides the base is too narrow, widens it with a frame and it stands.

subtype: Approach: asking a grandfather for tools and tips [Action]
passage: Jomon needed holes for the wheels of a wooden toy cart. In the yard he tried a nail, his hand slipped, and his thumb stung. "Dada, help me?" Ramesh Dada fetched a hand drill from the shed, set a block of wood under the plank and clamped it. "The block saves the table and your fingers," he said. "Now turn slowly." Jomon turned. The bit bit into the wood and dust curled up. They drilled four holes together and spent the afternoon fitting the wheels, Dada holding the axle straight while Jomon tapped it in.

qa.q: What did Ramesh Dada put under the plank?
qa.a: He put a block of wood under the plank.

qa.q: What was Jomon feeling after his thumb stung?
qa.a: Frustrated and a little hurt, and relieved to ask Dada for help.

qa.q: What could Jomon do next time a job needs a tool he does not know, and why?
qa.a: He could ask an adult first before trying it himself, since a safer way often exists.

qa.q: How does Ramesh Dada see Jomon's request?
qa.a: Ramesh Dada seems glad to be asked, and teaches carefully so they can finish the toy together.

grounding: A child who cannot make holes safely asks his grandfather, who shows a hand drill with a block underneath.

subtype: Approach: giving up when the first attempt fails [Pitfall]
passage: At the school field, thirty children lined up to fly their paper gliders in the wind. Rukmini's went straight down after two seconds and hit the grass nose first. Somebody snorted. "I'm just bad at making things," she said, crumpled the glider and sat on the bench. Her cousin Chinmay's glider crashed too, but Chinmay bent the wing tip, threw again, bent again. By the fourth throw it sailed right across the field. Rukmini watched from the bench with the ball of paper in her fist.

qa.q: What did Rukmini do with her glider after it crashed?
qa.a: She crumpled it and sat on the bench.

qa.q: What was Rukmini feeling when somebody snorted?
qa.a: Embarrassed and discouraged, which led her to decide she is bad at making things.

qa.q: What could Rukmini do next, and why?
qa.a: She could smooth the paper, bend the wings a little and throw again as Chinmay did, because each test shows what to change.

qa.q: How might Chinmay see a crashed glider?
qa.a: Chinmay treats a crash as information, bending the wing tip and throwing again until it flew.

grounding: A girl whose paper glider crashes decides she is bad at making things and stops, missing that adjusting improves the design.
